chapters.title: Chapter 4: Kelly Sizing in Indian F&O and Multi-Asset Portfolios

lessons.title: Portfolio-Level Kelly: Sizing Multiple Correlated Positions Together

children.text: Every lesson so far has sized one position at a time. Real accounts hold several positions at once, and those positions rarely move independently. A trader long Nifty futures and long a large private bank stock is not really holding two separate bets; a big share of both moves together. This lesson generalizes Kelly to handle exactly that.
Why You Can't Just Add Up Individual Kelly Fractions

Computing f* for each position separately and simply adding the fractions together gets the answer wrong in both directions. For two positions that move together, summing the individual fractions effectively doubles up on the same underlying risk, understating how much they behave like a single bet. For two positions that move independently, or better yet in opposite directions, summing individual fractions leaves real diversification benefit on the table, understating how much safe capacity the combination actually has.

The single-asset formula f* = μ/σ² from Lesson 2.3 generalizes directly to multiple assets held together. Let μ be the vector of each asset's expected excess return, and Σ the covariance matrix of their returns, capturing every asset's variance and every pairwise correlation at once.

body.caption: The vector of optimal fractions for each asset, accounting for how they move together

children.text: For two assets with equal volatility σ and correlation ρ, inverting the 2×2 covariance matrix by hand gives a clean closed form. Write k1 = μ1/σ² and k2 = μ2/σ² for each asset's own standalone Kelly fraction, computed as if it were the only position held.

body.caption: Equal-volatility special case. The full matrix formula handles unequal volatilities too.

children.text: Take two illustrative positions, both with 20% annual volatility: Nifty futures with an 10% expected excess return, and a large private bank stock closely tracking the index with an 8% expected excess return.

body.caption: How correlation reshapes the combined position

body.text: At ρ = 0.8, the bank stock's optimal fraction falls to exactly zero. Once a second position is correlated enough with a stronger-edge position, it stops adding anything the portfolio doesn't already have and gets crowded out entirely, not just downsized. Push correlation even higher with a weaker-edge asset and the formula can recommend a negative fraction: actively shorting the redundant, weaker position rather than holding it long at all. That is a genuinely advanced result and worth knowing exists, even if this lesson does not work through a full example of it.

body.title: Verify a row of the table
body.prompt: Using k1 = 2.50, k2 = 2.00, and ρ = 0.3, what is f2* = (k2 − ρk1) / (1 − ρ²)? Give your answer as a percentage, rounded to one decimal.

body.title: Explain the shrinking sum
body.scenario: A trader computes standalone full Kelly for two positions separately, gets 250% and 200%, and plans to hold both at once for a combined 450% leverage. The two positions are actually correlated at ρ = 0.6.
body.prompt: Using the table above, explain what is wrong with the trader's plan and what the properly adjusted combined leverage should be.
body.modelAnswer: Adding the two standalone fractions ignores that the positions move together. At ρ = 0.6, the properly adjusted fractions are 203.1% and 78.1%, for a combined 281.3%, well below the naively summed 450%. The 450% figure effectively treats two overlapping bets on the same underlying risk as if they were independent, understating how concentrated the true combined exposure actually is.

children.text: Applying Fractional Kelly and Translating to Rupees

Even after the correlation adjustment, 203.1% and 78.1% are still large numbers. Apply quarter-Kelly from Chapter 3 on top, exactly as with any other position, and convert to rupee targets for a ₹20,00,000 account.

body.caption: Quarter-Kelly on the ρ = 0.6 portfolio, ₹20,00,000 bankroll

children.text: Converting these targets into actual futures lots and shares uses exactly the mechanics from Lessons 4.1 and 4.2: divide by notional per lot or per share, and round down.

Beyond two assets, the by-hand algebra above becomes impractical, but the underlying formula, f* = Σ⁻¹μ, does not change. With five, ten, or fifty positions, this is computed with a full covariance matrix in code rather than worked out by hand, which is exactly how institutional desks approach multi-asset sizing in practice. The next lesson works through a full five-stock example this way.

body.title: Verify the ρ = 0.6 case with matrix inversion in Python

content.caption: numpy's matrix inverse applied to the 2-asset example
content.code:
import numpy as np

mu = np.array([0.10, 0.08])
sigma = 0.20
rho = 0.6

Sigma = np.array([
    [sigma**2, rho * sigma**2],
    [rho * sigma**2, sigma**2]
])

f_star = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) @ mu
print(np.round(f_star, 4))   # [2.0313, 0.7813] -> 203.13%, 78.13%

points: The single-asset formula f* = μ/σ² generalizes to f* = Σ⁻¹μ for a portfolio, where Σ is the full covariance matrix.
Summing standalone Kelly fractions overstates safe combined leverage for correlated positions and understates it for diversifying ones.
For two equal-volatility assets, f1* = (k1 − ρk2)/(1−ρ²), where k1 and k2 are each asset's own standalone Kelly fraction.
High enough correlation with a stronger-edge position can crowd a weaker-edge position's fraction all the way down to zero, or even negative, meaning the formula recommends shorting it.
Beyond two or three assets, this is computed in code with the full covariance matrix rather than by hand, exactly as Lesson 4.4 does for a five-stock portfolio.
